finding.claim: deleteAccount never enforces the ownership/admin check: canDelete(u, a) is called but its boolean result is discarded, so any authenticated user can delete any account by ID.
finding.source: Path parameter id (DELETE /accounts/{id}) and the caller's User u; precondition is a non-admin authenticated caller.

trace.note: deleteAccount(User u, long id) receives caller and target ID.
Account a = accounts.get(id) loads the target account.
canDelete(u, a) evaluated; boolean result discarded, no assertCanDelete call.

finding.guards_checked: canDelete (lines 9-11) implements admin-or-owner correctly but is not enforced here. closeAccount uses assertCanDelete (line 29), which is the missing pattern. No caller-identity check exists in this file; the User object's trustworthiness is unverified.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. canDelete (AccountService.java:9-11) is a correct admin-or-owner check, but deleteAccount calls it as a bare statement at line 22 and discards the boolean result. The throwing variant assertCanDelete (lines 13-17, used at line 29 in closeAccount) is not called on the delete path. No other file in the directory references deleteAccount, so no caller-side check is visible.
verdict.reason: At AccountService.java:22 canDelete(u, a) is a bare call whose boolean is discarded, so accounts.remove(id) at line 23 runs for any caller; the trace lines 20-23 match the code exactly. The attacker is any authenticated low-privilege user, and the only check is the missing one. The authentication of the User object itself is outside this file and is not verified here.

finding.claim: Null dereference in canDelete when the account does not exist lets a non-admin caller distinguish missing accounts from existing ones (account-ID enumeration oracle).
finding.source: Attacker-chosen id; precondition is an authenticated non-admin caller.
finding.sink: a.ownerId() at AccountService.java:10 when a is null.

trace.note: accounts.get(id) returns null for a missing ID (deleteAccount).
u.admin() is false, so a.ownerId() throws NullPointerException; an existing unowned account instead throws SecurityException at line 15 or returns normally.

finding.guards_checked: No null check on accounts.get(id) in deleteAccount or closeAccount, and none in canDelete. Response difference between missing and existing-but-unauthorized IDs is the oracle.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. The canDelete result at AccountService.java:22 is discarded as a bare statement, so it never blocks deleteAccount. The only check, assertCanDelete (line 13-17), is used only in closeAccount (line 29), not in the deleteAccount path. There is no null check on accounts.get(id) at line 21.
verdict.reason: For a missing ID, accounts.get(id) returns null at AccountService.java:21, canDelete(u, null) is called at line 22 with its result ignored, and a non-admin caller reaches a.ownerId() at line 10 and throws an NPE, while an existing account in deleteAccount is removed without any exception (line 23), so an authenticated non-admin can tell missing from existing IDs. The trace's line 15 SecurityException applies only to closeAccount (line 29), not to deleteAccount, so that one trace step is misapplied, though the core null-dereference path is accurate. The larger defect is that deleteAccount lets any authenticated user delete any account, because the discarded return value at line 22 means authorization is never enforced there.

finding.claim: closeAccount performs a permanent hard delete with no closed state, balance or activity check, or audit record, which may be a business-logic flaw depending on intended 'close' semantics.
finding.source: Path parameter id (POST /accounts/{id}/close); precondition is a caller that passes assertCanDelete.

trace.note: closeAccount(User u, long id) entry point.
Account a = accounts.get(id) loads the target.

finding.guards_checked: Ownership/admin check at line 29 is correct. No state-transition, balance, or audit controls exist. Whether hard deletion is intended is not determinable from the repo; low confidence.

verdict.guard_found: assertCanDelete (AccountService.java:29) calls canDelete (lines 13-17, 9-11), which throws SecurityException unless the caller is an admin or the account owner. The throw is not caught, so the remove at line 30 is only reached by an authorized caller.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code at lines 27-30, but the only callers who reach accounts.remove(id) at AccountService.java:30 are the account owner or an admin, who already have that power, and the guard at line 29 is effective. The remaining concern, that closing should be a soft state change rather than a hard delete, is a business-semantics question that the repo cannot settle and is not a security vulnerability.
